item.title: Crimea bridge shut after Ukrainian strike, as Russia hits Kyiv crossings
item.description:
Image caption,
Images circulated on social media appeared to show part of the road section of the Crimea bridge has collapsedByOlivia Ireland and Sarah Rainsford, Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, KyivPublished17 November 2026, 03:46 GMTUpdated 40 minutes ago
A key bridge linking occupied Crimea and Russia is closed after a Ukrainian strike inflicted major damage on the prized Kremlin asset.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials showed a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - had collapsed into the water.
Russian officials confirmed the structure had been damaged by drones, while Russia's deputy prime minister was due to chair an emergency meeting to discuss the situation.
Meanwhile, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.
Former Ukrainian adviser Anton Gerashchenko shared images and video footage appearing to show extensive damage to the road section of the Crimea bridge, with remnants of the support arch and road section seen protruding from the water below.
The bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.
While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the Crimea bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.
The timing of the Crimea bridge strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This strike could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
While the long-term impact of the strike on was not immediately clear, the bridge has been used to move troops and supplies into Crimea and towards the front line.

item.title: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
item.description:
Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty ImagesByMerlyn Thomas, BBC Verify correspondent and Paul Brown, BBC VerifyPublished4 hours ago
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.
Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.
The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.
With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.
Image source, DSNSImage caption,
Emergency service vehicles have also been targeted
Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".
He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

item.title: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Pakistan's ex-PM says doctors have warned that he is "highly vulnerable to ⁠a brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest"ByCaroline Davies, Pakistan correspondent and Kelly NgPublished8 hours ago
Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating.
"At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.
Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.
Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.
Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".
He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery.
"I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.
He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.
He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year.

item.title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex boss
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this yearByMichael Race and Osmond Chia, Business reportersPublished16 November 2026Updated 7 hours ago
Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.
Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.
But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.
The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance.
Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
Published4 days ago
The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process".
Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.

item.title: Body of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in Sydney skip bin
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
So You Are competing in the Melbourne Cup at Flemington Racecourse on 3 NovemberByClaire KeenanPublished3 hours ago
The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic.
In a video shared online, only two weeks after So You Are raced in the Melbourne Cup, the deceased racehorse appeared to be lying in a large metal bin surrounded by other household rubbish in Sydney.
Trainer Bjorn Baker - who shared news of the horse's death from colic on Monday - has said he was "deeply distressed" by the video, and called for a "full explanation".
Racing NSW, the state's industry regulator, said a preliminary investigation had found the horse was later properly buried, but called the way its body was handled "completely unacceptable".
"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in an statement shared online.
"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."
So You Are had a successful run during spring, winning four times at respected races including the Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.
The five-year-old recently finished eight in the Melbourne Cup, which was won by Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles III.
The racehorse had received urgent treatment after a severe bout of colic, but was "unfortunately unable to be saved" and was euthanised under anaesthesia, Racing NSW said.
"So You Are was then transported for burial, and was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when these images were recorded," it said.
Burial at a licensed landfill is typically recommended for animals that die from euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process, according to the racing body.
"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," it added.

item.title: Japan sends up jets after alleged Russian incursion of its airspace
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft were "completely unacceptable"ByKoh EwePublished2 hours ago
Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early on Tuesday.
South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones.
These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment.
The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump.
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable".
The last such incursion was in 2024, when a Russian military patrol plane entered Japanese airspace off Rebun island, Hokkaido.
Taiwan says its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, also on Tuesday.
South Korea says it sent up jets after an unspecified number of Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. The aircraft departed without violating South Korean airspace, authorities said.
It is unclear if the three neighbours were responding to the same or different aircraft.
The East China Sea contains self-declared, overlapping air defence identification zones between China, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea.
Foreign military aircraft are expected, but not legally required, to notify governments before entering such air defence identification zones.

item.title: Mozambique opposition leader faces trial over deadly 2024 election unrest
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Venâncio Mondlane was the runner-up in the 2024 presidential electionByJose Tembe, Reporting fromMaputo and Wycliffe MuiaPublished17 November 2026, 08:22 GMTUpdated 47 minutes ago
Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.
Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges, including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience, over protests that left hundreds of people dead. He denies any wrongdoing.
Security has been tightened around the Supreme Court, where Mondlane is due to appear on Tuesday, with authorities fearing a fresh wave of demonstrations by his supporters.
Police have appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly and avoid actions that could threaten public order.
The trial is widely seen as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after disputed elections triggered some of the country's deadliest political unrest in decades.
"The trial is a real test for Mozambique. It is is an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone," said Luis Nhachote, a political analyst.
Mondlane, who challenged the presidential election results that declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner, accused the authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages.
Children shot dead after joining pot-banging protests in Mozambique
Published23 November 2024
The demonstrations continued for months, with rights groups accusing security forces of using excessive force against protesters.
Amnesty International, citing local civil society organisations, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, which was one of the country's worst post-election crises since independence.

item.title: OpenAI sued by California over Hugging Face attack
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesByLily JamaliNorth America Technology correspondent, Reporting fromPalo Alto, CAPublished16 November 2026
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.
In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.
Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".
Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.
But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.
Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?
Published25 July
OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companies
Published29 July
Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.
The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.
Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.
"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.
OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.

item.description:

Watch: Forensic expert Michael Freeman speaks to Newsnight about Epstein's deathByTom McArthurBBC NewsPublished16 November 2026
This article contains distressing details and references to suicide
A forensic expert has said he believes that convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein's death in prison was the result of a homicide, not suicide.
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor Michael Freeman said that after reviewing the New York City medical examiner's file he believes Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind.
The medical examiner who carried out the autopsy concluded in 2019 that Epstein's injuries were consistent with suicide and there was no evidence of the defensive wounds expected if his death had been a homicide.
Epstein was found dead in prison on 10 August 2019 in New York as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.
Dr Barbara Sampson, chief medical examiner at the time of Epstein's autopsy, who ruled that Epstein's death was a suicide, has previously said: "I stand firmly behind our determination of the cause and manner of death for Mr. Epstein." The BBC has approached Sampson for further comment.
Freeman has served as a cause-of-death expert to attorneys-general in the US for death in police custody cases, including George Floyd in Minnesota.
He published his research and the New York City medical examiner's files after presenting his findings in London on Monday evening.
Freeman, who did not see the body, based his conclusions on the files and photographs from the examiner's report provided to him by Epstein's brother, Mark Epstein, who has always maintained that his brother was murdered.
Freeman said his analysis is independent and that he was not paid by Mark Epstein. His research has not been peer reviewed.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial next year for deaths of her three children
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: Date announced for Lindsay Clancy retrialByAna FaguyPublished16 November 2026
Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.
Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation.
The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face.
Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges.
Five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan were strangled at the family home on 24 January 2023. The defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis.
"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said at Monday's hearing.
Prosecutors wanted a May trial date, but Judge William Sullivan decided on March instead. The judge is due to retire in June.
Clancy was charged in the first trial with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.
The district attorney has not yet officially said he will proceed with first-degree-murder charges. The BBC has contacted the district attorney's office for comment.
